items.content:
Tor’s relay network is under a sustained circuit-creation DDoS. The attack floods volunteer relays with large numbers of client circuits, exhausting CPU, memory, and connection tables. It has been active in waves since at least late October 2026, with earlier related pressure in June through July.

The dominant techniques are high-volume circuit builds and BEGIN_DIR floods. BEGIN_DIR is the cell type used to request directory documents (consensus, descriptors) over an already-built circuit. Attackers open many circuits and issue these requests at rates that overwhelm the relay’s processing queue. Some variants produce extreme asymmetric traffic (high ingress or high egress), others drive tens or hundreds of thousands of connection attempts, and still others cause the relay to thrash while reporting relatively modest bandwidth. Operators have observed the method change within minutes of a mitigation or upgrade.

HSDir relays (those that store onion-service descriptors) have been particularly affected. Many lost the HSDir flag under load; some operators reported the attack on a given relay stopped the moment the flag was lost. Guard relays have also been hit. The result is degraded performance, temporary unreachability of some onion services, and reduced network capacity, though user anonymity itself is not reported as broken. This is a resource-exhaustion attack on the relays, not a deanonymization attack.

On 13 November the Tor Project released 0.4.9.17, an emergency update. The key change (TROVE-2026-031) alters IPv6 DoS accounting: instead of tracking every individual IPv6 address, relays now group clients by /64 prefix. Additional connection-isolation and data-validation fixes were included. The project stated that defending against the flood is not straightforward and that further releases should be expected. Relay operators are advised to upgrade immediately.

The attacker has already demonstrated adaptation. Multiple operators reported that after the 0.4.9.17 upgrade the traffic pattern shifted to a different technique within roughly ten minutes. Earlier defenses aimed at BEGIN_DIR and HSDir rate limits were also partially bypassed. No public attribution or claim of responsibility has been made.

The network continues to function because of roughly 9,000 volunteer relays, but the ongoing adaptive pressure is forcing repeated emergency releases and is visibly reducing the number of relays carrying certain flags.

items.content:
The microcode patch RAM on modern x86 is loaded before the first instruction the OS can see.

 Signature verification runs inside the sequencer. 

A voltage glitch timed to the compare step can force acceptance of an unsigned patch.

 The CPU continues with the modified behavior and the later cryptographic checks doesn't re-examine the already loaded patch.

items.content:
RT @SpiderMorpheus: Process Injection is one of the most fundamental capabilities of malware. It plays a role both in establishing a foothold after initial access and during post-exploitation, but the technique suffers from a fundamental problem: its traditional behavior is predictable and well understood by defensive solutions.

The classic Remote Process Injection flow can be roughly summarized in four stages:

1. Enumerate processes on the compromised machine;
2. Obtain a handle to the target process;
3. Allocate and write shellcode into the target process's memory space;
4. Change the memory region's permissions from RW to RX.

The set of WINAPIs designed for these operations is relatively small, which makes life easier for EDRs. The list of the most sensitive APIs is short:

VirtualAllocEx → NtAllocateVirtualMemory
VirtualProtectEx → NtProtectVirtualMemory
WriteProcessMemory → NtWriteVirtualMemory

Whether through kernel callbacks or userland hooks on ntdll, these calls are easily monitored. There are ways to deal with this problem, including simply not performing process injection, at least not during initial access, and choosing something like DLL Sideloading. But we want a challenge, right? :)

In the screenshot I show something different. It is possible to write into a remote process's memory without invoking sensitive APIs such as NtAllocateVirtualMemory or NtWriteVirtualMemory.

Based on an article written by the amazing researcher @TwoSevenOneT, I developed a shellcode runner that successfully evades Windows Defender (with Cloud-Delivered Protection enabled) by poisoning a target process hStdInput. The technique abuses Windows console applications (such as netsh.exe) by redirecting the child process's hStdInput handle via CreateProcess with STARTF_USESTDHANDLES. The content written to the Named Pipe ends up allocated in the target process's memory by the operating system itself, with no explicit call to VirtualAllocEx or WriteProcessMemory.

To locate the shellcode in remote memory, the payload is preceded by a previously established byte sequence that serves as a marker. The runner scans the target process's memory for this pattern, identifies the region, adjusts permissions, and redirects execution to the shellcode.

None of the most sensitive APIs are used for writing the payload. Three APIs that are also used, among other purposes, in traditional injection are present (VirtualProtectEx, CreateProcessW, and ResumeThread), but outside their traditional context they are far less suspicious.

Currently, this shellcode runner PoC would not successfully evade top-tier EDRs, but the goal was to demonstrate viability, not perfection. A little bit more evasion tomfoolery would be enough.

The link to the article that guided me through this experiment will be down below, make sure to do something useful with your life and read it.

Keep Hacking,
